newsitem.title: USA: Stocks roar despite gloomy earnings outlook.
newsitem.headline: Stocks roar despite gloomy earnings outlook.

text.p: Stocks are zooming into record territory on the prospects that the Federal Reserve will hold interest rates unchanged, and for now, investors are not overly worried that third-quarter earnings growth could be the weakest in five years.
While the second-quarter earnings of the Standard & Poor's 500 companies rose an unexpectedly strong 10.1 percent due to a strong economy, a smaller economic tailwind is seen for the third quarter.
First Call, which tracks corporate earnings estimates, said the growth in earnings year-over-year may increase by just 6.1 percent, which would be the smallest rise since the fourth quarter of 1991.
The third-quarter earnings season will start in mid-October.

Results will likely be negatively impacted by slowing economic growth, the experts said. Gross domestic product growth for the third quarter is seen at 2.5 percent, down from the second quarter's estimated 4.8 percent pace.
"I'm concerned about my third-quarter earnings forecasts," said Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities.

"The consumer is slowing down, there's no pricing power yet and there's some inventory buildup," she said. "Interest rates are up and the economy is slowing -- not a good combination for 1997 earnings either."

Nevertheless, the mood on Wall Street was still upbeat as the blue-chip Dow Jones industrial average celebrated news that inflation was still in check, which should mean that the Fed will keep interest rates unchanged.
On Monday, the 30-stock index closed up a solid 50.68 points at a new high of 5,889.20, beating Friday's record close of 5,838,52.
The Standard & Poor's 500 index jumped 3.44 points to a new high of 683.98.

The stampede to buy stocks accelerated with last week's news that the Producer Price Index edged up 0.3 percent in August and the Consumer Price Index inched up just 0.1 percent, confirming that inflation was still dormant.
The speculation was widespread that the central bank would pull the interest-rate trigger at the Sept. 24 meeting of the policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee.

David Shulman, chief equity strategist at Salomon Brothers, said he does not expect third-quarter results "to knock down the market as a whole," as was the case in the second quarter, when some companies warned that they would have disappointing results.
"The test is the next two weeks," with more earnings pre-announcements, he said.

So far, only a handful of companies have warned that their earnings for the latest quarter would be sub-par. The list includes Rubbermaid Inc., Ben & Jerry's Homemade Inc., ITT Corp. and Procter & Gamble Co. and Kellogg Co. and Digital Equipment Corp.
Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter, was more optimistic than others on earnings and stock market prospects.

He said that Dean Witter on Monday cut the cash asset allocation in its basic asset portfolio by 5 percent from 25 percent, and raised its stock holdings to 60 percent from 55 percent and left bonds at 20 percent.
"My guess is not only will third-quarter earnings be good, but the fourth quarter will be even better after a lousy fourth quarter last year. That reinforces the upward movement in the market.

"The interest rate outlook is much more important than whatever earnings have been -- that'll determine what earnings will be," Canelo said. "If it's less threatening, you can't get over-bearish over profits."
